extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers / self-published authors who want to write a novella
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, step-by-step guidance for planning, writing, and editing a novella (a short fiction book between a short story and a novel), with advice on structure, pacing, POV, cast, and form suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length / word count
rubrics_metrics.description: A novella is a fiction book that is shorter than a novel, but longer than a short story. It is usually between 20,000 and 50,000 words, or about 100-200 formatted pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page also states a related range elsewhere: "a novella is usually between 10,000 to 40,000 words." Note that these numbers can vary based on formatting (font size, margins, printer) and publisher decisions; use the word-count ranges as guidelines rather than absolute rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish by complexity (not just word count)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main difference between novelette, novella, and novel is word count, but also the complexity of plot and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As you move from novelette → novella → novel, elements should grow more complex: more subplots, more dynamic characters, deeper/conflicting motivations, expanded worldbuilding and themes. Use complexity expectations to inform whether your idea fits a novella or needs a longer/shorter form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Become familiar with novellas (read widely)
rubrics_metrics.description: Read as many novellas as possible, particularly in the genre you want to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take notes about how the stories unfold, what makes them strong or weak, what appeals to you, and which ones resemble your concept. Studying examples helps you understand pacing, structure, and device choices suited to the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide on the type of novella (literary / inspirational / genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novellas typically fall into one of three categories: literary, inspirational, and genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary novellas are usually character-driven, deeper, and aim to teach a point (example: Home by Toni Morrison). Inspirational novellas are often shorter and parable-like (appeal to younger readers). Genre novellas (fantasy, sci‑fi, mystery, action-adventure, erotic romance) focus on plot/world or a focal relationship; knowing your type clarifies tone, pacing, and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully plan a concise outline
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a novella outline because a concise story and low word count are hallmarks of the format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your outline can be anything that suits your style (quick bullet points, scene-by-scene summary, etc.). Planning prevents scope creep and helps you fit a complete arc into a compact space; you can use novel-writing software to structure and flesh out the outline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick one central conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: A novella should generally only have one central conflict to keep the plot focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the main question or conflict: What is happening to your protagonist? What must they overcome? What is the Call to Adventure and how will it be delivered? How will the conflict be resolved within limited space? Limiting to one central conflict helps maintain clarity and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pacing must be balanced: the story can’t drag nor feel rushed given the novella’s shorter space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure tension, conflict, and intrigue are paced to keep readers engaged. Avoid a slow first half followed by a cramped second half (or vice versa). Pacing choices should be intentional—sometimes slow, uncomfortable pacing is a deliberate stylistic choice (the Factory example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the story from one clear point of view and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose and stick to a single narrative point-of-view and time (first/second/third; present/past) for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using one POV and timeline reduces confusion in a condensed work and preserves narrative focus; decide this before writing so voice and tense remain consistent throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep your cast small
rubrics_metrics.description: Pare down characters—omit stock or flat characters and anyone who doesn’t clearly move the plot or the protagonist’s arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what character types your novella needs, which arcs you’ll focus on, how characters will change, and whether secondary characters have essential arcs. Fewer, well-developed characters suit the novella’s economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit intentionally; prioritize precision
rubrics_metrics.description: With fewer words, your prose must be stronger and more precise—editing is crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise with language, use metaphors effectively, and ensure themes/morals are conveyed despite brevity. Learn to love the editing process and don’t rush revision; tighter prose will carry more weight in a shorter form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage symbolism, motifs, and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelettes and novellas often rely more heavily on symbolism, motifs, metaphors, and imagery to tell the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because space is limited, use evocative devices to convey depth and theme without lengthy exposition. Symbolic and imagistic writing can enrich a compact narrative efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the story suits the novella form
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your story is suited to a novella; some projects naturally expand to novels or compress to short stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It’s fine if a project changes length during writing—let the story/characters determine the necessary space. Choosing the novella form should be intentional, based on whether the concept fits a single central conflict, limited cast, and compact arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and page-count considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Page counts depend on formatting decisions such as font size, margins, and printer requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting word count to pages (e.g., ~80–200 pages cited), remember formatting choices will alter final page numbers; consider formatting during the book-design step and when planning length for publishing.
